clue.text: One who beats others in many games of bridge

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a crossword stock for 'many'
a rubber is a set of games, best of three, at bridge

explanation.surface: A card player who keeps winning hand after hand at the bridge table.
explanation.walkthrough: D for 'many' comes from the Roman numerals. The surface wants the whole clue to be about bridge; only the last three words are.
explanation.definitionFit: To drub is to thrash or defeat soundly, so a drubber is someone who trounces opponents.

clue.text: Ruthless competition producing cannibalism?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom for cut-throat rivalry
second meaning, taken literally: one canine devouring another

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the literal second reading of a familiar idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock idiom for merciless rivalry, and read word by word it describes animals eating their own kind.

clue.text: Perfect early C on piano, perhaps

parts.note: ut was the original name of the first note of the scale, later called do (C)

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the word could be arranged otherwise, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A pianist playing a flawless C early in a piece.
explanation.walkthrough: In Guido's medieval sol-fa, the notes were ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la; ut was later renamed do, the C of the major scale.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopian describes an ideal, flawless state of affairs, as in More's imagined perfect island.

clue.text: Make prohibitions in great numbers in Eastern city

parts.note: to ban is to prohibit
galore means in abundance

explanation.surface: An authority issuing prohibitions by the score somewhere in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link here, not an instruction to put one piece inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Bangalore (now Bengaluru) is a large city in southern India, in the East from a British viewpoint.

clue.text: Inadequate as a painter might be

definitions.meaning: first meaning: informal British for poor or of low quality

definitions.note: a comparison phrase standing for an adjective
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a painter is the rope at a boat's bow used for tying up, so it is rope-like

explanation.surface: An artist whose work is not up to scratch.
explanation.walkthrough: A painter is also a boat's mooring line. 'Ropey' (also spelt ropy) is British slang for shoddy or unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both shoddy in British slang and resembling cord, which describes a mooring line.

clue.text: Whacking very sound sleepers in tents

parts.note: whacking is informal for very large
from the phrase 'sleep like a top', to sleep very soundly

explanation.surface: Campers sleeping soundly under canvas, with whacking hinting at some violence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whacking' reads as a verb of hitting; here it is the adjective meaning huge.
explanation.definitionFit: Big tops are the large marquees used by circuses, so they are a kind of tent.

clue.text: Reverie in a room at Rugby

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a state of deep absent-minded thought
second meaning: the study of Tom Brown, hero of Tom Brown's Schooldays, set at Rugby School

explanation.surface: A pupil lost in daydreams in a room at his boarding school.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby is the English public school in Thomas Hughes's novel Tom Brown's Schooldays, where senior boys had their own studies.
explanation.definitionFit: A brown study is an idiom for being lost in thought, a daydreaming state.

clue.text: Habitual exaggerator's swans.

parts.note: surface reading: the swans owned by a boastful person
setter's reading: an old proverb says that everything a boaster owns is grander in his telling, so his so-called swans are really humbler farmyard birds

explanation.surface: A boaster showing off his supposedly magnificent swans.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'all his geese are swans' is said of someone who always exaggerates the worth of his own things.
explanation.definitionFit: What the boaster calls swans are really common farmyard birds, the humbler waterfowl of the saying.

clue.text: Both parts of round, trip in wild area

parts.note: first half of a round trip: the outward leg
second half of a round trip: the return leg

explanation.surface: Both legs of a return journey into the wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: A round trip goes out and comes back; the comma is there to disguise the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The outback is the remote, sparsely populated interior of Australia, the wild bush country.

clue.text: Scrap or discard right in the middle

indicators.note: placing a letter in the middle means the other word is split around it

parts.note: to shed is to cast off or discard
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Choosing whether to throw something away or keep it in the centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap or discard' looks like a pair of synonyms; only 'Scrap' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A shred is a tiny torn strip, so a scrap or fragment of something.

clue.text: Wrong parts for adult

indicators.note: the word broken into parts and put back together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An actor playing an adult role he is unsuited to.
explanation.definitionFit: Grown-up and fully developed: a grown person is an adult, adjective for adjective.

clue.text: Demonstrator for old silver coin

parts.note: pro means in favour of
a tester (teston) was a Tudor silver coin worth sixpence

explanation.surface: Someone showing off products, asked to accept an antique coin as payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' looks like a link word between definition and wordplay but gives letters itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A protester joins a demonstration, so a demonstrator in the political sense, not someone showing a product.

clue.text: One of Napoleon's equals? At first, anyway

definitions.text: One of Napoleon's equals? At first, anyway

parts.note: surface reading: a peer of the French emperor
setter's reading: Napoleon is the pig in Orwell's satire, whose farm began with every creature declared equal before some became more equal than others

explanation.surface: Who could rank alongside the French emperor, at least at the start of his career?
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon is the pig who takes over in Orwell's Animal Farm, whose commandment 'All animals are equal' later gains 'but some are more equal than others'.
explanation.definitionFit: Every creature on Orwell's farm was a beast declared equal, before the pigs rewrote the commandment.

clue.text: Popular at home? Damned odd, that is

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

indicators.note: odd means strange or irregular, so the following word is put out of its normal order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone surprised to find themselves sought after while sitting at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' sits after the word it acts on: it is the anagram signal, not a comment on the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sought after by many people is wanted widely, which is what being popular amounts to.

clue.text: Small amount of money tied up in Oxford, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a very small budget, as in running a business on a tiny sum
second meaning: an Oxford is a style of laced shoe, fastened with a lace

explanation.surface: A modest sum of money invested in the university town of Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' is not the city but a lace-up shoe; 'tied up' means knotted, not invested.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something on a shoestring means doing it with a tiny budget; a shoelace is tied up in an Oxford shoe.

clue.text: Two rings needed for this wild beast

parts.note: first ring: a ding is the ringing sound of a bell
second ring: the letter O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A circus trainer needs two rings to show off his wild animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two rings' supplies two different kinds of ring: one heard, one seen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian wild dog is an untamed animal, so a wild beast in the plainest sense.

clue.text: How striker brought about his own dismissal

definitions.text: How striker brought about his own dismissal

parts.words: How striker brought about his own dismissal
parts.note: surface reading: a worker on strike who got himself sacked
setter's reading: in cricket the striker is the batsman facing the bowling, out when he knocks down his own stumps

explanation.surface: An industrial striker got himself fired by his own actions.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batsman facing the ball is 'the striker'; if he knocks the bails off his own stumps while playing a shot, he is out in this way.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the recognised ways a batsman can be given out, entirely by his own doing.

clue.text: Get into debt — without any interest

parts.note: to incur a debt is to get into it
IOUs are written promises to pay, records of debt

explanation.surface: Borrowing money from a lender who charges no interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without any interest' looks like a loan term; it means lacking curiosity.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uninterested and lacking curiosity is incurious, showing no wish to know more.

clue.text: Name on act as legal document

parts.note: a title is a name, as of a book
a deed is an act

explanation.surface: Putting a name on a statute to make it a legal document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'act' suggests an Act of Parliament; here it is a plain synonym for something done.
explanation.definitionFit: A title deed is the formal paper proving ownership of property, a document with legal force.

clue.text: Port wine to conclude

parts.note: Graves is a Bordeaux wine region and its wine
to end is to conclude

explanation.surface: Finishing a meal with a glass of port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port wine' reads as one drink; 'Port' is the definition and 'wine' starts the wordplay. Gravesend is a town on the Thames estuary in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kent town has long been a harbour on the Thames, a place where shipping docks.

clue.text: One flies from Canada via Toronto

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, rather than built up

parts.note: spanning the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A traveller flying out of Canada by way of Toronto.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is a pilot, a person who flies aircraft.

clue.text: Space traveller to regain consciousness, almost

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter of the phrase is dropped

parts.note: to come to is to regain consciousness

explanation.surface: An astronaut coming round after a blackout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come to' loses its final O.
explanation.definitionFit: These icy bodies travel through the solar system on long orbits, so they journey across space.

clue.text: Disorder in a port, an Italian one

definitions.note: the comma sits between the parts of the definition

parts.note: a mess is a state of disorder
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Chaos breaking out in an Italian harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a' gives letters directly; the definition is 'port, an Italian one'. Messina is a port in Sicily, on the strait between it and the mainland.
explanation.definitionFit: Messina is a Sicilian harbour city, and Sicily belongs to Italy, so it is an Italian seaport.

clue.text: Another jack from the same deck

definitions.text: Another jack from the same deck

parts.words: Another jack from the same deck
parts.note: surface reading: a second jack from one pack of playing cards
setter's reading: a jack is a sailor and the deck is a ship's deck, so this is a fellow crew member

explanation.surface: Drawing a second jack from a pack of cards.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack (as in Jack Tar) is a sailor, and deck belongs to a ship rather than a card pack.
explanation.definitionFit: A fellow sailor serving aboard the same vessel is your crewmate, another seaman on that deck.

clue.text: Workers employed to record score

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the employees of an organisation
second meaning: the five lines on which music is written

explanation.surface: Employees hired to keep the tally at a sporting match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' is a musical score, not a match result.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm's personnel are its employees, and the musical stave on which notes are written is also called by this name.

clue.text: Fruit bat, nothing more

parts.note: uncertain: no standard sense of bat gives these letters
O, the shape of zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A fruit bat, described as nothing more than that.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is unclear: O for 'nothing' is standard, but no usual sense of bat yields the rest. The answer is fixed by every crossing letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The mango is a sweet tropical stone fruit, eaten fresh or in chutney.

clue.text: Character from Selkirk, originally

parts.note: surface reading: someone born in the Scottish Borders town of Selkirk, or a letter taken from the start of its name
setter's reading: Alexander Selkirk, the marooned sailor whose story inspired Defoe's novel

explanation.surface: A local personality born in the Scottish town of Selkirk.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Selkirk was marooned on a Pacific island for four years; Defoe based Robinson Crusoe on him. 'Originally' tempts a first-letter reading, but no letters are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Defoe's castaway hero is a fictional figure modelled on the real Scottish sailor.

clue.text: Maiden — she's silly to become engaged

parts.note: M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for a maiden over

indicators.note: silly means foolish or muddled, so the word before it is put into a muddled order

parts.note: taken as written; the apostrophe-s is read as 'is', linking to the indicator

explanation.surface: A young woman being foolish enough to get betrothed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engaged' suggests a wedding but means interlocking, as gears do. In cricket a maiden is an over with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: When gears mesh their teeth interlock, which is the mechanical sense of becoming engaged.

clue.text: Heedful, and tentative moving at first

indicators.note: with 'at first', moving tells us to shift the little word at to the front of the next word
first says where the shifted pair of letters ends up: at the very front

parts.note: taken as written; it contains the pair of letters at

explanation.surface: Someone careful and hesitant in their first steps.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'tentative moving at first' literally: take the AT out of TENT-AT-IVE and put it first, giving AT + TENTIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying close heed means watching and listening carefully, which is what an attentive person does.

clue.text: Provide view round tree

parts.note: O is round in shape
the pine is a tree

explanation.surface: A view across the landscape around a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' here does not ask for one piece to go round another; it gives a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To opine is to state an opinion, offering your view on something.

clue.text: Two sorts of coats in the distance

parts.note: first sort: a fur coat
second sort: a long coat

explanation.surface: Two different coats glimpsed far off.
explanation.definitionFit: A furlong is an eighth of a mile, a unit of length still used in horse racing.

clue.text: Something maid doesn't have to manage

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a maid, an unmarried woman, has no spouse
second meaning: to ... resources is to manage them thriftily

explanation.surface: A list of things a housemaid need not take care of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maid' is the old sense of an unmarried girl, not a servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A married man is the spouse an unmarried woman lacks; as a verb it means conserving and administering resources carefully.
